title: Huge Pages — Hardware Support
summary: Trading page granularity for TLB reach — how a handful of huge pages can cover what thousands of regular pages couldn't.

slides.markdown:
**Huge pages** (2MB or 1GB, versus the standard 4KB) let a single TLB entry cover far more memory at once. Since TLB reach is entries × page size, making the page size 512× bigger (2MB vs 4KB) means the same TLB entry count covers 512× more memory.

For large, contiguous working sets — big in-memory databases, large ML tensors, virtual machine memory — this can be the difference between a TLB that comfortably covers the whole working set and one that's constantly missing.

slides.subTitle: The TLB-reach limit
slides.markdown:
TLB reach (entries × page size) is often surprisingly small — a 64-entry TLB with 4KB pages covers only 256KB, far less than a typical L2 cache. A program with a large working set (say, gigabytes of data it touches repeatedly) will constantly TLB-miss even though the *data* itself might comfortably fit in L2 or L3 cache.

This mismatch means a program can be cache-friendly but still pay heavily for translation overhead, purely because the TLB can't keep up with how much memory the program actively touches.

slides.subTitle: Fewer, bigger entries
slides.markdown:
The same memory region that needs hundreds of 4KB-page TLB entries can be covered by a single 2MB-page entry instead.

![The same memory region covered by many 4KB TLB entries versus a single 2MB entry](assets/huge-page-tlb-coverage.svg)

Fewer entries means far fewer TLB misses for the same working set — the trade is coarser granularity for much better TLB coverage.

assets.alt: The same memory region covered by many 4KB TLB entries versus a single 2MB entry

slides.subTitle: Multiple page sizes at once
slides.markdown:
Hardware supports huge pages by allowing a page-table entry at an intermediate level to terminate the walk early — rather than pointing to yet another level of the tree, it directly marks "this entry covers a 2MB (or 1GB) region" and gives the frame number right there.

This means a single page table can mix page sizes freely: most of a process's address space might use standard 4KB pages while a specific large buffer uses 2MB pages, all resolved through the same walking mechanism, just terminating at a different level depending on the page's declared size.

slides.subTitle: Huge pages vs regular pages
slides.markdown:
| | Regular pages (4KB) | Huge pages (2MB / 1GB) |
|---|---|---|
| TLB pressure | Higher for large working sets | Much lower |
| Internal fragmentation | Minimal | Can be significant |
| Allocation flexibility | Fine-grained | Coarse — must allocate in large chunks |
| Best for | General-purpose, varied allocations | Large, dense, long-lived allocations |

Huge pages win decisively for large, contiguous, heavily-touched memory. They lose for workloads with lots of small, short-lived, or sparse allocations, where the coarser granularity wastes memory and allocation becomes awkward.

slides.subTitle: Huge pages aren't a free performance win
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Huge pages always improve performance, so enable them everywhere."

**Why it's wrong:** a 2MB page is one solid unit — if an app needs only a fraction, or allocates sparsely, the rest is wasted **internal fragmentation** for its whole lifetime. Allocating one also needs 2MB of physically *contiguous* memory, which can fail or force costly compaction.

**Correct model:** huge pages target large, dense, long-lived regions (databases, VM memory) — not a default. Applied to sparse allocations, they can waste more than the TLB savings are worth.
